lesson.menu_title: The Day I Decided to Leave
lesson.menu_desc: The Tuesday that ended one life and started another -- telling the story with the two past tenses that carry a narrative
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 6 -- The Day I Decided to Leave
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Ana Claudia Veraldi | Lesson 6 -- The Day I Decided to Leave

listenings.text: I can tell you the exact date, which people always find slightly odd. It was the fourteenth of March, and I was sitting in my car on the same road I sat on every single morning of my working life. Completely gridlocked. Nothing was moving in either direction. The radio was playing something cheerful, which did not help at all. And I looked down at the clock and worked out that I had been in that car for fifty five minutes and had travelled about a mile and a half. That was the last straw, honestly. It was not the worst morning I had ever had. It was simply the morning where something snapped. I did nothing reckless, you understand. I drove to the office, I sat through three meetings, and I went home. But that evening I told my wife, and six weeks later I handed in my notice. My mother tried very hard to talk me out of it.

Everybody talks about the moment of deciding. Nobody talks about the eight months afterwards, and that is where the difficulty actually lives. I decided on a Sunday, in about four minutes, while I was washing up. It felt wonderful. And then for the rest of that year I had second thoughts roughly every second week. My brother told me I was burning my bridges. A colleague said I was being reckless at forty three. I very nearly did not go through with it. Twice. What finally helped was something my grandmother said to me. She said, you are not deciding whether to be happy, you are deciding which problems you would rather have. So I chose the new problems. I have never once wanted the old ones back. But I want to be honest with you: it was not a brave decision taken on a whim. It was a frightened decision taken very slowly.

extra_audio.text: Can I ask what actually made you do it, in the end? There was one Tuesday. I was sitting in traffic and the road had not moved in forty minutes. And that was the moment? That was the last straw, yes. Something just snapped. Did anyone try to stop you? Everybody. My brother spent a month trying to talk me out of it.

vocab.title: Match each word to its meaning
defs: The final small problem that makes you act, after many others
So blocked by traffic that nothing moves at all
Acting without thinking about the risk
The moment where an important change begins
To become clear to somebody for the very first time
To suddenly lose your patience after holding it for a long time

vocab.text: Two of tonight's twelve are whole phrases, not single words: the last straw and to burn your bridges. Keep them intact, exactly as they are. Somebody who drops the last straw into a story at the right moment sounds like a person who has been telling stories in English for years.

reading.rtitle: Nobody Leaves a City on a Tuesday
paras: Ask people why they left the city and they will rarely give you a reason. They give you a day. They were standing in a lift, or waiting in a supermarket queue, or sitting in a car that had not moved for forty minutes, and something very small happened. That small thing became the last straw.

Researchers who study these decisions call the moment a turning point, and they notice the same shape every time. Nothing dramatic was happening. Life was going on exactly as it always had. Then, one entirely ordinary Tuesday, something snapped, and the person who had been accepting a situation for eleven years simply stopped accepting it.

What follows is rarely reckless, even though it looks that way from the outside. Very few people act on a whim. They go home, they sit down, and they spend weeks doing arithmetic. Friends try to talk them out of it. Somebody always says they are burning their bridges. And a great many of them have second thoughts at three in the morning, more than once.

But the ones who go through with it describe the same thing afterwards. It was not courage, they say, and it was not a plan. It was simply that on one particular day, while everything around them was carrying on as usual, it dawned on them that they did not have to keep living that way. They handed in their notice a week later. The Tuesday, they insist, was the easy part.

reading.prompt: Read once, quickly. Which title fits the whole text best?
choices: Why big cities are worse places to live than small towns
The decision looks sudden from outside, but the leaving is slow and full of doubt
Most people who leave the city end up regretting it

items: People usually explain the move with a clear reason.
The opposite. They rarely give you a reason — they give you a day, one specific Tuesday.
Something dramatic was normally happening at the moment of the decision.
Nothing dramatic was happening. Life was going on exactly as it always had.
Friends often try to persuade the person not to go.
Friends try to talk them out of it, and somebody always says they are burning their bridges.
The people who left describe the decision as an act of courage.
It was not courage, they say, and it was not a plan.
Many of them still have doubts after they have decided.
A great many of them have second thoughts at three in the morning, more than once.

items.situation: A new colleague asks how you ended up living so far from Sao Paulo. Start the story with the background, not with the decision.
tips: I was sitting in traffic on an ordinary Tuesday, and nothing was moving.
Set the scene in past continuous first, then drop the event in.

items.situation: Somebody asks what the actual moment was. Name it in one sentence.
tips: That was the last straw. Something just snapped.
Past simple — the moment is a point, not a background.

items.situation: A colleague says it sounds like you did it on a whim. Correct them, politely.
tips: It looked like a whim. It was not.
Then say how long it actually took.

items.situation: Somebody asks whether anybody tried to stop you.
tips: My brother spent a month trying to talk me out of it.
Everybody told me I was burning my bridges.

items.situation: A German colleague admits she is having second thoughts about the same move. Answer honestly, not with encouragement.
tips: I had second thoughts every week for a year.
That is not a sign that you are wrong.

items.situation: You are asked what you were doing at the exact moment you decided.
tips: I was driving home, the radio was playing, and it just dawned on me.
Two past continuous verbs, then one past simple.

answerkey.title: Reveal the whole narrative key
key: past continuous (was / were + -ing) = the background, already running: it was raining and nobody was moving
past simple = the event that moves the story on: then my phone rang
when + past simple = the interruption: I was sitting in traffic when the call came
while + past continuous = the long action the event lands inside: while I was waiting, I decided
two past continuous = two long actions at the same time: she was cooking while I was packing
past simple in sequence = one thing after another: I stood up, walked out and drove home
STATIVE verbs never take -ing: I knew, I wanted, I understood — never I was knowing
NEVER: I was deciding to leave · when I was sitting, the phone was ringing · I was knowing
